name: Mechanical automatic watch

lead: An automatic watch is a mechanical watch that winds itself. A weighted rotor swings with the wearer's arm and tightens the mainspring, so no battery is needed. People wear them as a style accessory; the watch is a visible part of a put-together look.

As gear, it adds to overall presentation rather than changing any physical feature. Looks communities discuss watches under accessories and style, and some wearers value the visible mechanism and craftsmanship.

paras: The watch is worn daily so the rotor keeps the mainspring wound; many can also be wound by hand with the crown. A fully wound mainspring typically runs about two days. Wearers pair case size, strap and dial colour with their outfit and wrist size.

No health risks beyond ordinary strap or metal skin sensitivity. Mechanical movements are less accurate than quartz, need occasional servicing, and can be damaged by shocks or magnetism. Prices range widely.

angle.text: The watch is a visible accessory that people use to complete an outfit and signal taste. It affects presentation, not facial or body structure.

lead: An automatic (self-winding) watch is a mechanical wristwatch in which the wearer's movement turns an oscillating weight, or rotor, that winds the mainspring through a ratchet and gear train.[1] It is worn mainly as a style accessory and is covered in appearance communities alongside other watches and jewellery.

The idea dates to the late 18th century, when Abraham-Louis Perrelet made the earliest credible self-winding pocket watch. John Harwood's 1923 patent produced the first commercially successful automatic wristwatch, and Rolex later introduced a rotor that turns a full 360 degrees.[1]
By the 1960s automatic winding was common in quality mechanical watches.[1] As gear for looks, the watch contributes to outfit coordination and a polished impression rather than altering the body.

paras: Wrist motion swings the rotor, whose rotation winds the mainspring. A slipping bridle, patented by Adrien Philippe in 1863, prevents overwinding. Most automatics can also be hand-wound via the crown.[1]
A fully wound mainspring typically runs the watch for about two days.[1]

Perrelet's design of about 1776-77 is regarded as the earliest credible self-winding watch, and Breguet and Hubert Sarton produced rotor designs soon afterwards.[1] Harwood's bumper-weight wristwatch was produced in roughly 30,000 units before his company collapsed in 1931; Rolex followed with a full-rotation rotor around 1930-31.[1]

Watches appear in community discussion of accessories as part of style. One Lemmy user even described their automatic Swatch as a cue for how long they had been away from home, an example of the watch used as a routine marker.[2]

timeline.event: Perrelet makes the earliest credible self-winding pocket watch.[1]
Adrien Philippe patents the slipping bridle.[1]
Harwood patents the first commercially successful automatic wristwatch.[1]
Harwood's company collapses; Rolex rotor design emerges around this time.[1]
